chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
title: The roughest place: Funky Butt Hall
summary: Ory describes a dance hall that was also a church, where razors and guns were common.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: What was the roughest place around town that you remember playing?

The roughest place? It was, uh, used to be an old church on Padilla Street. It changed two or three times. And sometimes when, uh, dance would get, go down, you know, then they'd go out there open for a Baptist church, you see. Some pretty jack-legged preacher was coming in with a big sign, reverence, so-and-so, you know. And he'd preach his half away, then someone would come back and open for a dance hall. After all, it's called the Funky Butt Hall. Funky Butt Hall. Yeah. Was that a pretty tough place? Huh? Tough place, huh? Tough. Tough place I ever played. What happened? Well, if you didn't have a razor or a gun, you couldn't get him.
What part of town was that? But they didn't live with it. Oh, yeah.
I played there once. Just once, huh?
Was there fighting going on and so on while you were playing? Oh, yeah.
On the sidewalk in the hall.

I wish you'd see the place. I'd look. The record of the old barn, you know, out in the country for Satan. The place. Who gave parties there? Who promoted that place? They did dance. Anyone you could rent. Anybody could rent it. Yeah. I tell you, it went from Baptist Church back there. Dance hall, Baptist Church. Thanks. Doug.
